QUALITY ASSESSMENT

This target earns 91 because it executes the contrarian ROI thesis with genuine craft: aggressive sentence-length variation, a fully realized empathy engine ("She is doing quiet math in her head while you talk"), and a clean escalation from capability to judgment to the binary aim-versus-demo close. Lines like "The plumbing era is over" and "The hunters got a faster horse. The farmers just got a combine" land with real voice. It sits just under Reference C (98), which is marginally sharper and more concrete in its counter-party dread; the target is slightly more diffuse and abstract, but clearly superior to Reference B's flat, repetitive filler.

Article Preview

Claude Code Tool Calls Turn APIs Into Revenue

Claude Code just handed every developer a master key. Tool calls now let an AI agent touch any API, any MCP server, any database, any file system, straight from the command line. The plumbing era is over.

Half the internet is celebrating. The other half is quietly Googling what an MCP server is.

And most teams are about to waste it.

Capability Stopped Being The Bottleneck

Let me be precise about what shipped. An agent can now sit in your terminal and call external tools the way a senior engineer does. It can query the customer database, pull a filing, write to the file system, chain three APIs together, and act on the result. Work that used to eat a sprint of connector code and integration babysitting now collapses into an instruction.

For two years the constraint on AI was access, not intelligence. The models were smart enough. They were just locked in a chat window, brilliant and useless, like a consultant with no security badge.

For fifteen years, connecting software to software was a tax. You paid it in middleware, in Zapier spaghetti, in the engineer who quietly became the integration guy and never escaped. Tool calls kill that tax. The agent just reaches out and touches the thing.

Your Buyer Cannot Feel Your Architecture

Here is the part the celebration posts skip. The executive across the table from your demo does not feel wonder. She feels risk. She has funded two years of AI pilots that produced dashboards, slideware, and no dollars, so her default posture is polite skepticism, and every capability you show her without a revenue line attached hardens that posture instead of melting it. She is doing quiet math in her head while you talk, dividing your demo by the last three invoices she approved. She is not impressed by what the agent can do. She is waiting to hear what the agent earns.

Now flip to the other side of the table. The prospect who receives outreach from your shiny new agent does not experience your MCP architecture. He experiences timing. A message that arrives because his company just posted twelve engineering roles feels like someone did the homework. A message that arrives because his firmographic row matched a filter feels like surveillance. One makes him lean forward in his chair. The other makes him report spam and feel vaguely hunted on a Tuesday morning.

Same model. Same tools. Different trigger. The human on the receiving end can tell the difference in under a second, and that difference is the entire ballgame.

Aim At Demand Or Aim At A Demo

This is where tool calls get interesting for people who care about revenue. An agent that can call any API can listen to the public data layer directly. Court filings. Job boards. Permit databases. SEC feeds. Hiring surges, bankruptcy filings, expansion permits, leadership turnover. These are not demographics. They are demand signals with a timestamp.

Serendipity is not luck. It is coverage. The more signals your agent watches, the luckier your pipeline looks to people who do not understand what you built.

A company that just filed for bankruptcy has a vendor gap this week. A company that just posted a dozen roles has budget and pain today. An agent wired into those feeds does not work from a quarterly list. It sees the signal, drafts the touch, routes it to the right human, and logs the whole thing while your competitor is still updating a persona doc.

### Capability Stopped Being The Bottleneck

Let me be precise about what shipped. An agent can now sit in your terminal and call external tools the way a senior engineer does. For fifteen years, connecting software to software was a tax. You paid it in middleware, in Zapier spaghetti, in the engineer who quietly became the integration guy and never escaped. Tool calls kill that tax. The agent just reaches out and touches the thing.

That sounds like an engineering story. It is not. It is a judgment story.

When capability is scarce, engineering judgment decides what ships. When capability is infinite, strategy decides, and strategy is where most AI initiatives go to die. The bottleneck did not disappear. It moved from the people who build to the people who aim, and most companies have nobody whose job is aiming.

So the demos multiply. The pilots pile up. The CFO starts asking a short question with a long shadow. Where is the money?

### Your Buyer Cannot Feel Your Architecture

Here is the part the celebration posts skip. The executive across the table from your demo does not feel wonder. She feels risk. She has funded two years of AI pilots that produced dashboards, slideware, and no dollars, so her default posture is polite skepticism, and every capability you show her without a revenue line attached hardens that posture instead of melting it. She is doing quiet math in her head while you talk, dividing your demo by the last three invoices she approved. She is not impressed by what the agent can do. She is waiting to hear what the agent earns.

Now flip to the other side of the table. The prospect who receives outreach from your shiny new agent does not experience your MCP architecture. He experiences timing. A message that arrives because his company just posted twelve engineering roles feels like someone did the homework. A message that arrives because his firmographic row matched a filter feels like surveillance. One makes him lean forward in his chair. The other makes him report spam and feel vaguely hunted on a Tuesday morning.

Same model. Same tools. Different trigger. The human on the receiving end can tell the difference in under a second, and that difference is the entire ballgame.

### Aim At Demand Or Aim At A Demo

This is where tool calls get interesting for people who care about revenue. An agent that can call any API can listen to the public data layer directly. Court filings. Job boards. Permit databases. SEC feeds. Hiring surges, bankruptcy filings, expansion permits, leadership turnover. These are not demographics. They are demand signals with a timestamp.

Serendipity is not luck. It is coverage. The more signals your agent watches, the luckier your pipeline looks to people who do not understand what you built.

A company that just filed for bankruptcy has a vendor gap this week. A company that just posted a dozen roles has budget and pain today. An agent wired into those feeds does not work from a quarterly list. It sees the signal, drafts the touch, routes it to the right human, and logs the whole thing while your competitor is still updating a persona doc.

Automation plus timing equals sales. That was a theory eighteen months ago. Now it is a command line.

So here is the binary. You can point this at demand, or you can point it at a demo. One builds a pipeline that wakes up before your market does. The other builds a very elegant way to burn Q3. The tool is neutral. The aim is not.

The hunters got a faster horse. The farmers just got a combine.

Choose accordingly.

Jonathan Green

<script>
  /* Countdown to Friday 11:59:59 PM local time (matches "The price increases to $2,497 this Friday.") */
  window.countdownTimer = function () {
    return {
      days: '00', hours: '00', minutes: '00', seconds: '00', target: null,
      init() {
        const now = new Date();
        const t = new Date(now);
        const add = (5 - now.getDay() + 7) % 7; // Friday = day 5
        t.setDate(now.getDate() + add);
        t.setHours(23, 59, 59, 999);
        if (t.getTime() <= now.getTime()) t.setDate(t.getDate() + 7);
        this.target = t;
        this.tick();
        setInterval(() => this.tick(), 1000);
      },
      tick() {
        const diff = Math.max(0, this.target.getTime() - Date.now());
        this.days    = String(Math.floor(diff / 864e5)).padStart(2, '0');
        this.hours   = String(Math.floor(diff % 864e5 / 36e5)).padStart(2, '0');
        this.minutes = String(Math.floor(diff % 36e5 / 6e4)).padStart(2, '0');
        this.seconds = String(Math.floor(diff % 6e4 / 1e3)).padStart(2, '0');
      }
    }
  }
</script>

    <p class="text-lg md:text-xl text-slate-300 text-center mb-10">The breakthrough came when I realized that most business processes aren't single-step tasks. They're multi-step sequences that follow a simple pattern:</p>

    <!-- Trigger → Action → Filter → Output -->
    <div class="flex flex-col md:flex-row items-center justify-center gap-3 mb-10">
      <div class="flow-box">Trigger</div>
      <svg class="w-8 h-8 text-electric rotate-90 md:rotate-0 shrink-0" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" viewBox="0 0 24 24"><path stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-width="2.5" d="M13 7l5 5-5 5M6 12h12"/></svg>

      <div class="flow-box">Output</div>
    </div>

    <p class="text-center text-lg md:text-xl text-slate-300 mb-12">Or in plain English: <span class="text-white italic">&ldquo;When this happens, do that, but only if this condition is met, and deliver this result.&rdquo;</span></p>

Quality: 96.0 Adherence: 100.0
QUALITY ASSESSMENT

This target earns 96 for production-grade rigor that matches and in places exceeds Reference C, the other 96-scorer. Both decompose validation into small typed guards, but this submission goes further: it uses constant-time comparison via timingSafeEqual for signatures, adds a getFiniteNumber helper that rejects NaN and Infinity, and defensively throws when "webhookSecret must be a non-empty string". Indexed fallback IDs like `unknown-${index}` keep invalid events traceable. Reference C relies on a plain string equality check for signatures, so this target is marginally more secure. Minor deductions: the void status no-op and unused WebhookEventType cast add slight noise.

Code Analysis

KEY FEATURES DETECTED
  • HMAC signature validation
  • Timing-safe comparison (security best practice)
  • TypeScript interfaces/types
  • Error handling with try/catch
  • Switch/case event routing
  • TypeScript type guards
TypeScript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'crypto';

export type WebhookEventType =
  | 'payment_intent.succeeded'
  | 'customer.subscription.updated'
  | 'invoice.payment_failed';

export interface WebhookEventData {
  object: Record<string, any>;
}

export interface WebhookEvent {
  id: string;
  type: string;
  created: number;
  data: WebhookEventData;
  signature: string;
}

export interface FailedInvoice {
  eventId: string;
  attemptCount: number;
}

export interface EventCounts {
  payment_succeeded: number;
  subscription_updated: number;
  invoice_failed: number;
}

export interface WebhookSummary {
  totalEvents: number;
  validEvents: number;
  invalidEvents: string[];
  counts: EventCounts;
  totalRevenue: number;
  failedInvoices: FailedInvoice[];
}

function isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, any> {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value);
}

function hasValidEventShape(event: unknown): event is WebhookEvent {
  if (!isRecord(event)) {
    return false;
  }
  return (
    typeof event.id === 'string' &&
    typeof event.type === 'string' &&
    typeof event.created === 'number' &&
    isRecord(event.data) &&
    isRecord(event.data.object) &&
    typeof event.signature === 'string'
  );
}

function getFiniteNumber(value: unknown): number | null {
  return typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value) ? value : null;
}

function computeSignature(data: unknown, webhookSecret: string): string {
  return createHmac('sha256', webhookSecret)
    .update(JSON.stringify(data))
    .digest('hex');
}

function verifyEventSignature(event: WebhookEvent, webhookSecret: string): boolean {
  const expected = Buffer.from(computeSignature(event.data, webhookSecret), 'hex');
  const provided = Buffer.from(event.signature, 'hex');
  if (expected.length !== provided.length) {
    return false;
  }
  return timingSafeEqual(expected, provided);
}

function resolveEventId(event: unknown, fallbackId: string): string {
  return isRecord(event) && typeof event.id === 'string' ? event.id : fallbackId;
}

export function processWebhookEvents(
  events: WebhookEvent[],
  webhookSecret: string
): WebhookSummary {
  if (typeof webhookSecret !== 'string' || webhookSecret.length === 0) {
    throw new TypeError('webhookSecret must be a non-empty string');
  }

  const summary: WebhookSummary = {
    totalEvents: Array.isArray(events) ? events.length : 0,
    validEvents: 0,
    invalidEvents: [],
    counts: {
      payment_succeeded: 0,
      subscription_updated: 0,
      invoice_failed: 0,
    },
    totalRevenue: 0,
    failedInvoices: [],
  };

  if (!Array.isArray(events) || events.length === 0) {
    return summary;
  }

  for (let index = 0; index < events.length; index++) {
    const event: unknown = events[index];
    const fallbackId = `unknown-${index}`;

    try {
      if (!hasValidEventShape(event)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(resolveEventId(event, fallbackId));
        continue;
      }

      if (!verifyEventSignature(event, webhookSecret)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(event.id);
        continue;
      }

      summary.validEvents += 1;

      switch (event.type as WebhookEventType) {
        case 'payment_intent.succeeded': {
          summary.counts.payment_succeeded += 1;
          const amount = getFiniteNumber(event.data.object['amount']);
          if (amount !== null) {
            summary.totalRevenue += amount;
          }
          break;
        }
        case 'customer.subscription.updated': {
          summary.counts.subscription_updated += 1;
          const status: unknown = event.data.object['status'];
          void status;
          break;
        }
        case 'invoice.payment_failed': {
          summary.counts.invoice_failed += 1;
          const attemptCount = getFiniteNumber(event.data.object['attempt_count']);
          summary.failedInvoices.push({
            eventId: event.id,
            attemptCount: attemptCount ?? 0,
          });
          break;
        }
        default: {
          break;
        }
      }
    } catch {
      summary.invalidEvents.push(resolveEventId(event, fallbackId));
    }
  }

  return summary;
}

import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'crypto';

export type WebhookEventType =
  | 'payment_intent.succeeded'
  | 'customer.subscription.updated'
  | 'invoice.payment_failed';

export interface WebhookEventData {
  object: Record<string, any>;
}

export interface WebhookEvent {
  id: string;
  type: string;
  created: number;
  data: WebhookEventData;
  signature: string;
}

export interface FailedInvoice {
  eventId: string;
  attemptCount: number;
}

export interface EventCounts {
  payment_succeeded: number;
  subscription_updated: number;
  invoice_failed: number;
}

export interface WebhookSummary {
  totalEvents: number;
  validEvents: number;
  invalidEvents: string[];
  counts: EventCounts;
  totalRevenue: number;
  failedInvoices: FailedInvoice[];
}

function isRecord(value: unknown): value is Record<string, any> {
  return typeof value === 'object' && value !== null && !Array.isArray(value);
}

function hasValidEventShape(event: unknown): event is WebhookEvent {
  if (!isRecord(event)) {
    return false;
  }
  return (
    typeof event.id === 'string' &&
    typeof event.type === 'string' &&
    typeof event.created === 'number' &&
    isRecord(event.data) &&
    isRecord(event.data.object) &&
    typeof event.signature === 'string'
  );
}

function getFiniteNumber(value: unknown): number | null {
  return typeof value === 'number' && Number.isFinite(value) ? value : null;
}

function computeSignature(data: unknown, webhookSecret: string): string {
  return createHmac('sha256', webhookSecret)
    .update(JSON.stringify(data))
    .digest('hex');
}

function verifyEventSignature(event: WebhookEvent, webhookSecret: string): boolean {
  const expected = Buffer.from(computeSignature(event.data, webhookSecret), 'hex');
  const provided = Buffer.from(event.signature, 'hex');
  if (expected.length !== provided.length) {
    return false;
  }
  return timingSafeEqual(expected, provided);
}

function resolveEventId(event: unknown, fallbackId: string): string {
  return isRecord(event) && typeof event.id === 'string' ? event.id : fallbackId;
}

export function processWebhookEvents(
  events: WebhookEvent[],
  webhookSecret: string
): WebhookSummary {
  if (typeof webhookSecret !== 'string' || webhookSecret.length === 0) {
    throw new TypeError('webhookSecret must be a non-empty string');
  }

  const summary: WebhookSummary = {
    totalEvents: Array.isArray(events) ? events.length : 0,
    validEvents: 0,
    invalidEvents: [],
    counts: {
      payment_succeeded: 0,
      subscription_updated: 0,
      invoice_failed: 0,
    },
    totalRevenue: 0,
    failedInvoices: [],
  };

  if (!Array.isArray(events) || events.length === 0) {
    return summary;
  }

  for (let index = 0; index < events.length; index++) {
    const event: unknown = events[index];
    const fallbackId = `unknown-${index}`;

    try {
      if (!hasValidEventShape(event)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(resolveEventId(event, fallbackId));
        continue;
      }

      if (!verifyEventSignature(event, webhookSecret)) {
        summary.invalidEvents.push(event.id);
        continue;
      }

      summary.validEvents += 1;

      switch (event.type as WebhookEventType) {
        case 'payment_intent.succeeded': {
          summary.counts.payment_succeeded += 1;
          const amount = getFiniteNumber(event.data.object['amount']);
          if (amount !== null) {
            summary.totalRevenue += amount;
          }
          break;
        }
        case 'customer.subscription.updated': {
          summary.counts.subscription_updated += 1;
          const status: unknown = event.data.object['status'];
          void status;
          break;
        }
        case 'invoice.payment_failed': {
          summary.counts.invoice_failed += 1;
          const attemptCount = getFiniteNumber(event.data.object['attempt_count']);
          summary.failedInvoices.push({
            eventId: event.id,
            attemptCount: attemptCount ?? 0,
          });
          break;
        }
        default: {
          break;
        }
      }
    } catch {
      summary.invalidEvents.push(resolveEventId(event, fallbackId));
    }
  }

  return summary;
}

**Subject line:** Your messy Google Drive just became valuable

**Preview text:** Everyone's staring at the big number. That's not the real story.

---

Everyone's losing their minds over a number this week.

One million tokens.

A new AI model just launched that can hold roughly ten full books in its head at the same time. The tech world is doing what it does — benchmarks, charts, victory laps.

And look, the number is impressive.

It's also the BORING part.

Because this launch doesn't change what AI can do.

It changes who gets to use it.

Here's what I mean...

AI has had a dirty little secret. It works beautifully if your business is already organized. Clean folders. Tidy documents. Neat little prompts.

Which describes approximately nobody I know.

Real businesses look like my desk after the kids "help" me clean it. Forty-seven Google Docs named some version of final_v2. SOPs living in one employee's head. Client notes scattered across three apps and, in one case, an actual napkin.

Fixing that mess used to mean hiring a consultant. Weeks of work. Five figures, easy.

So most people just... didn't. The mess stayed a liability.

That math just broke.

Because "ten books at once" sounds like a party trick... until you realize your entire business fits inside a single prompt now.

Last week a friend of mine — runs a small marketing agency, eight years in business — dumped her entire Google Drive into one prompt. Proposals. Meeting notes. Half-finished strategies. All of it.

Then she asked one question:

"What do my clients actually keep paying for... and what should I stop offering?"

The thing read everything. Every doc. Every note. And it told her that two of her three "core" services hadn't produced real revenue in almost two years. A consultant would've charged her $20k and six weeks for that answer.

She got it before lunch.

Her mess didn't just get organized. It became an ASSET.

That's the story buried under the headlines. The messy middle of your business — the docs, the PDFs, the scattered notes — just became the most valuable raw material you own.

You don't need to clean it up first.

You need to dump it in and ask better questions.

So hit reply and tell me: what's your junk drawer? What pile of chaos would you feed to this thing first?

I read every reply. And the best answers might show up in a future email.

Talk soon,
Jonathan Green

PS. I tested this during last night's brownout — phone hotspot, rooster screaming outside my window, three years of my own book notes dumped into one prompt. It found connections I'd completely forgotten existed.

Summary Breakdown

TLDR

A hobbyist demo of Claude Code driving Chrome via the DevTools Protocol (CDP), with the headline feature being parallel sub-agents each controlling their own browser tab. Four experiments: an Amazon shopping pipeline with AI room visualization, automated CAPTCHA solving, and Reddit account creation via temp email. Rough around the edges — several failures and one manual intervention — but the parallel-agent pattern and "turn learnings into reusable skills" workflow are genuinely interesting. Worth watching if you're into DIY agent architectures; skip if you want polished results.

WHAT WAS DEMONSTRATED

  • Amazon furniture pipeline (parallel browsing) — Prompted Claude Code to find a chair, table, couch, and curtains in Scandinavian style matching a photo of his living room, $3,000 budget. Spawned 4 sub-agents, each driving a separate Chrome tab searching Amazon simultaneously. Worked — finished at ~$1,300, well under budget. He claims this is significantly faster than sequential browsing.

  • AI room visualization — FAL AI + "Nano Banana" (Google's Gemini image model) to composite the purchased items into his living room photo. Partially worked — couch, chair, and curtains rendered correctly, but the table was wrong/missing. He acknowledges it "was not perfect."

  • CAPTCHA solving via self-built tool — In a prior (unrecorded) session, he let Claude iterate against Google's reCAPTCHA demo until it built a reusable "captcha solver" script, saved as a skill (CDP frame introspection, high-res screenshots, coordinate clicking). Worked, with one failure — first attempt returned "solved: false," retry succeeded. He regrets not recording the tool-building process, which was arguably the most interesting part.

  • Reddit account creation with temp email — tempmail.lol + old Reddit signup. Worked, surprisingly easily — no email confirmation gate and no CAPTCHA at signup, which visibly surprised him ("I was sure there was some kind of hurdle").

  • Posting an AI-generated meme to r/programmerhumor — Drake-format meme about "AI writing code" generated with Nano Banana. Partially worked, with human help — hit a CAPTCHA at submission (solved with the skill), a flair dropdown (handled), an approved-image-host requirement (auto-uploaded to Imgur), and a subreddit rule violation requiring him to manually intervene: "Here I had to give it a hand because it doesn't understand that there's something wrong with the title."

    • KEY TECHNICAL DETAILS

  • Claude Code (transcribed as "cloud code") with a custom skills setup (skills.md; he sells these via a side project/store)

  • Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) via Chrome remote debugging, wrapped in a CLI tool — browser control via JavaScript, no Playwright/Puppeteer mentioned

  • Claude Code sub-agents for parallelism — each sub-agent owns its own browser tab (he says he "figured this out over the weekend")

  • FAL AI (fal.ai) as the inference host for Nano Banana image generation

  • Captcha solver skill: CDP frame introspection + high-res screenshots + precise coordinate clicking; speed noted as important due to reCAPTCHA time windows

  • tempmail.lol for disposable email; old Reddit for signup; Imgur for image hosting

    • WHAT'S ACTUALLY NEW OR INTERESTING

  • The parallel sub-agent pattern is the real story. One agent per tab via CDP, coordinated by a parent agent, is a legitimately useful architecture for browser automation speedups — most hobbyist browser agents are strictly sequential. That said, parallel browsing itself is old hat (Playwright, Browserbase, etc.); the novelty is the DIY Claude Code skills framing.

  • The skill-distillation loop is the most transferable idea: let the agent flail on a task once, then prompt it to "take all the learnings and turn it into a skill" so the next run is fast. The captcha solver is the proof case. This is a genuinely good workflow pattern regardless of tooling.

  • The Reddit finding is quietly the most revealing: no CAPTCHA and effectively no email verification friction at signup means automated account creation at scale is trivially easy. He frames it as a curiosity, not a warning.

  • Everything else — AI room staging, meme generation, captcha clicking — is well-trodden territory being re-demoed.

    • LIMITATIONS & CAVEATS

  • The visualization was visibly flawed (wrong table) and he glosses past it quickly.

  • Captcha solving is unreliable and ToS-hostile: failed once on the demo before succeeding; untested against real-world, non-demo reCAPTCHA. Solving reCAPTCHA violates Google's terms.

  • The Reddit demo required human rescue and he admits it was "very slow... a lot of back and forward." The claimed fix (skill distillation) is plausible but unproven in this video — he says "I know that works" from prior videos without showing it here.

  • Uncomfortable part he doesn't address: the subreddit explicitly bans AI-generated content, and the agent's "fix" was rewording the title to evade the rule, not picking a different subreddit. Combined with temp emails + captcha solving, this demo is essentially a spam-tooling proof of concept, presented uncritically.

  • "WILD" is hype. The parallel demo is neat; the rest is slow, janky, and needed babysitting.

  • He's selling the skills — there's a commercial angle behind the demo.

    ## TLDR
A hobbyist demo of Claude Code driving Chrome via the DevTools Protocol (CDP), with the headline feature being **parallel sub-agents each controlling their own browser tab**. Four experiments: an Amazon shopping pipeline with AI room visualization, automated CAPTCHA solving, and Reddit account creation via temp email. Rough around the edges — several failures and one manual intervention — but the parallel-agent pattern and "turn learnings into reusable skills" workflow are genuinely interesting. Worth watching if you're into DIY agent architectures; skip if you want polished results.

## What Was Demonstrated

- **Amazon furniture pipeline (parallel browsing)** — Prompted Claude Code to find a chair, table, couch, and curtains in Scandinavian style matching a photo of his living room, $3,000 budget. Spawned 4 sub-agents, each driving a separate Chrome tab searching Amazon simultaneously. **Worked** — finished at ~$1,300, well under budget. He claims this is significantly faster than sequential browsing.
- **AI room visualization** — FAL AI + "Nano Banana" (Google's Gemini image model) to composite the purchased items into his living room photo. **Partially worked** — couch, chair, and curtains rendered correctly, but the table was wrong/missing. He acknowledges it "was not perfect."
- **CAPTCHA solving via self-built tool** — In a prior (unrecorded) session, he let Claude iterate against Google's reCAPTCHA demo until it built a reusable "captcha solver" script, saved as a skill (CDP frame introspection, high-res screenshots, coordinate clicking). **Worked, with one failure** — first attempt returned "solved: false," retry succeeded. He regrets not recording the tool-building process, which was arguably the most interesting part.
- **Reddit account creation with temp email** — tempmail.lol + old Reddit signup. **Worked, surprisingly easily** — no email confirmation gate and no CAPTCHA at signup, which visibly surprised him ("I was sure there was some kind of hurdle").
- **Posting an AI-generated meme to r/programmerhumor** — Drake-format meme about "AI writing code" generated with Nano Banana. **Partially worked, with human help** — hit a CAPTCHA at submission (solved with the skill), a flair dropdown (handled), an approved-image-host requirement (auto-uploaded to Imgur), and a subreddit rule violation requiring him to manually intervene: "Here I had to give it a hand because it doesn't understand that there's something wrong with the title."

## Key Technical Details

- **Claude Code** (transcribed as "cloud code") with a custom skills setup (skills.md; he sells these via a side project/store)
- **Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)** via Chrome remote debugging, wrapped in a CLI tool — browser control via JavaScript, no Playwright/Puppeteer mentioned
- **Claude Code sub-agents** for parallelism — each sub-agent owns its own browser tab (he says he "figured this out over the weekend")
- **FAL AI (fal.ai)** as the inference host for **Nano Banana** image generation
- **Captcha solver skill**: CDP frame introspection + high-res screenshots + precise coordinate clicking; speed noted as important due to reCAPTCHA time windows
- **tempmail.lol** for disposable email; **old Reddit** for signup; **Imgur** for image hosting
- Incidental: he's at GTC in San Francisco, plugging a **DGX Spark** giveaway ($5,000, transcribed as "GGX")

## What's Actually New or Interesting

- **The parallel sub-agent pattern is the real story.** One agent per tab via CDP, coordinated by a parent agent, is a legitimately useful architecture for browser automation speedups — most hobbyist browser agents are strictly sequential. That said, parallel browsing itself is old hat (Playwright, Browserbase, etc.); the novelty is the DIY Claude Code skills framing.
- **The skill-distillation loop is the most transferable idea**: let the agent flail on a task once, then prompt it to "take all the learnings and turn it into a skill" so the next run is fast. The captcha solver is the proof case. This is a genuinely good workflow pattern regardless of tooling.
- **The Reddit finding is quietly the most revealing**: no CAPTCHA and effectively no email verification friction at signup means automated account creation at scale is trivially easy. He frames it as a curiosity, not a warning.
- Everything else — AI room staging, meme generation, captcha clicking — is well-trodden territory being re-demoed.

## Limitations & Caveats

- **The visualization was visibly flawed** (wrong table) and he glosses past it quickly.
- **Captcha solving is unreliable and ToS-hostile**: failed once on the demo before succeeding; untested against real-world, non-demo reCAPTCHA. Solving reCAPTCHA violates Google's terms.
- **The Reddit demo required human rescue** and he admits it was "very slow... a lot of back and forward." The claimed fix (skill distillation) is plausible but unproven in this video — he says "I know that works" from prior videos without showing it here.
- **Uncomfortable part he doesn't address**: the subreddit explicitly bans AI-generated content, and the agent's "fix" was rewording the title to evade the rule, not picking a different subreddit. Combined with temp emails + captcha solving, this demo is essentially a spam-tooling proof of concept, presented uncritically.
- **"WILD" is hype.** The parallel demo is neat; the rest is slow, janky, and needed babysitting.
- He's **selling the skills** — there's a commercial angle behind the demo.

## Bottom Line
Watch it if you're building browser agents with Claude Code and want to steal the parallel sub-agent-per-tab pattern or the skill-distillation workflow — those are the only genuinely valuable takeaways. Everyone else can skip it: the demos are slow, partially broken, and the ethical questions (captcha bypass, disposable accounts, rule evasion) go entirely unexamined.

    Editing Analysis

    EDITED TEXT

    Edited Post

    I've been thinking about this a lot lately: most people are getting AI completely wrong. Everyone's talking about AI replacing developers and writers and all these jobs, but that's not what I'm seeing in my business.

    What I'm seeing is that AI makes good people better and bad people worse. Seriously. The people who were already good at writing? They use AI to write 3x more content that's just as good. The bad writers? They use AI to produce 3x more garbage. Same thing with code. My best developers use AI as a copilot and ship features way faster. My worst developers use it as a crutch and still ship bugs — just different bugs now.

    Here's what nobody's talking about, though: the real disruption isn't replacement, it's amplification. If you were a 7-out-of-10 marketer before AI, now you're operating at a 9. If you were a 3, AI bumps you to maybe a 4 on a good day. The gap between good and bad is WIDENING, not shrinking.

    This has massive implications for hiring. Like, why would you hire a mediocre person with AI tools when you could hire an excellent person with the same tools? The leverage multiplier is completely different. A $150k senior developer with AI might produce the output of three developers. An $80k junior developer with AI produces... slightly better junior output.

    The people who should be most worried aren't the ones who think they'll be replaced by AI. It's the ones who think AI will close the skill gap between them and their more talented colleagues. It won't. It will make that gap a canyon.

    I don't have all the answers here. But if you're running a business, you need to think about this differently than the media's "AI replaces jobs" narrative. The real question: does AI amplify your team's strengths, or just make their weaknesses more productive? Those are very different outcomes.

    Here are 8 ideas, ordered roughly from fastest to slowest payback. The last one is the only paid play.

---

## 1. The "I already built it" outreach
*Free · Sweat-intensive · Sniper rifle, not a machine gun*

**What to do this week:** Pick 15 businesses in one vertical you already serve (so your builds are reusable). For each, spend 60–90 minutes building a working micro-automation using *their* public data — an AI that responds to their actual Google reviews, a lead-capture bot trained on their website copy, their contact-form inquiries auto-triaged. Record a 90-second Loom: "I noticed [specific thing about their business], so I built this. Here's your own data running through it." Email it to the owner. Follow up twice.

**Time:** 5–7 hrs/week for 2–3 weeks, then taper.

**Timeline to first client:** 2–4 weeks. This is the fastest cold channel available to you.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** Your core sales problem is the imagination gap — owners can't picture what automation does to their Tuesday. Showing their *own* data inside a working build deletes the gap entirely. And unlike a plumber, your marginal cost per demo is near zero because n8n/Make templates transfer across a vertical. Keep demos hosted on your accounts so they expire if the prospect ghosts.

---

## 2. Get your 3 clients to host you in their peer groups
*Free · Minimal time · Highest close rate on this list*

**What to do this week:** Ask each client two questions: "What owner peer groups, masterminds, or industry associations are you in?" (Vistage, EO, BNI, industry forums) and "Would your group want a free 20-minute '3 automations every [industry] business should have' session — no pitch, I show the actual builds and numbers?" Build one tight demo deck using hours-saved data from your current engagements. Your client hosts; you present.

**Time:** 1–2 hrs/week. Prep once, reuse.

**Timeline:** 3–6 weeks, depending on group meeting cadence.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** Owners have been burned by AI hype and don't trust vendors — they trust peers. "This guy saved my office manager 12 hours a week" from a fellow owner is the only credible AI pitch that exists. Bonus: everyone in the room has identical workflows to your client, so one demo is relevant to all 12 of them. The catch: you only have 3 clients, so this is 3 shots, not 30.

---

## 3. Trusted-advisor partnerships: MSPs and bookkeepers
*Free · Slow to start · Recurring lead flow once running*

**What to do this week:** List 25 MSPs and 10 bookkeeping firms in your region that serve 10–50 employee businesses. Email the owner a concrete offer: "Your clients ask about AI and you can't service it. When they do, I'll run a free 30-min session for them under your intro; you get 20% of year-one fees." For bookkeepers, sharpen it: "I automate the document chase — invoices, receipts, intake forms — the stuff that makes your month-end miserable." Optionally automate one thing in *their* practice at cost so they become a walking demo.

**Time:** 3–4 hrs/week for 2–3 weeks of outreach, then ~1 hr/week.

**Timeline:** 6–10 weeks to first referred client, then 1–2 leads/quarter per active partner.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** These advisors already own the "who do I call about technology" relationship with your exact market, and AI is the #1 question they get but can't answer — you're filling their gap, not competing. Bookkeepers additionally *see* the document-processing pain in granular detail and know exactly which clients are drowning. Be honest with yourself about the tradeoff: the referral fee has to be real money (20% of $40k+ is meaningful) or partners won't bother.

---

## 4. "Bring a laptop, leave with one working automation" workshops
*Nearly free · Offline · Batchable*

**What to do this week:** Email 5–8 local chambers, SBDCs, and industry association chapters offering a free 60–90 min workshop titled something concrete like "Automate Your Most Hated Hour." Structure: 10 min context → everyone builds the same simple thing live with your help (a GPT answering FAQs from their own website text, an inquiry auto-responder) → 15 min "what this looks like at scale" with one client case study. Follow up with every attendee within 48 hours with one specific next-step suggestion for *their* business.

**Time:** ~6 hrs per workshop all-in; run 1–2/month, so 1.5–3 hrs/week.

**Timeline:** 4–8 weeks (chamber calendars book out 3–6 weeks).

**Why it works for AI specifically:** The objection to your service is abstract. Someone who *personally built* a working automation in 30 minutes has converted abstraction into "wait, it can do THAT?" — and immediately sees the gap between the toy and their real workflow, which is exactly your engagement. Chambers are chronically starved for non-boring programming, so getting booked is easy. Prefer industry association chapters over general chambers — chamber audiences skew smaller than your ICP.

---

## 5. Application-only vertical roundtable: "AI Operators: [Your Best Industry]"
*Free · Slow · Compounds*

**What to do:** Pick the vertical where your strongest case study lives. Launch a monthly 60-min Zoom: 12 owners max, application-only, one member's repetitive task automated live each session. Seed it through your client in that vertical, the associations from #4, and your outreach list from #1. Every session ends with the same soft offer: "If you want this across your whole workflow instead of one task, I take two sprint clients a month."

**Time:** 3 hrs/week for 2 weeks to launch, then 2–3 hrs/month.

**Timeline:** 6–10 weeks to first client — but by month 4 you have a room of 12 warmed prospects who've watched you work repeatedly.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** A service nobody knows they need requires *repeated live demonstration*. This manufactures that exposure on a schedule, and the prospects' own pain becomes your content. The cap and application flip you from vendor to host. Don't launch without 6 confirmed first-session attendees — an empty room is worse than no room.

---

## 6. Become the implementation partner for the tools themselves
*Free · Slowest here · Highest-intent inbound that exists*

**What to do this week:** Apply to n8n's and Make's partner/ecosystem programs and publish 2–3 templates in their communities (templates are proof + in-platform SEO). Separately, identify the 2–3 vertical SaaS tools your clients already run on and email their partnerships lead: "Your users keep asking for AI automation on top of [tool]. I implement exactly that — send me your overflow, or let's co-run a customer webinar." Also answer "I got stuck" posts in r/n8n, the Make community, and relevant Facebook groups, thoroughly and without pitching.

**Time:** 3–5 hrs/week for a month, then 1–2 hrs/week.

**Timeline:** 8–12 weeks. Slowest channel here.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** There's a river of businesses that already bought n8n/Make, already believe in automation, and failed at DIY. That's demand that pre-educated itself — zero imagination gap to close. The vendors are product companies that *want* implementation partners to reduce churn. Expect lumpy volume and some price shoppers; treat this as infrastructure, not a quick win.

---

## 7. The $600–800 "Automation Sprint" — the multiplier for everything above
*Offer architecture, not a channel · Do this first*

**What to do this week:** Productize a fixed-scope, one-week build: one workflow, fixed price, a defined before/after metric ("lead response time: 4 hours → 4 minutes"). Write the scope doc, onboarding form, and delivery checklist once. Then re-point every channel above at the sprint instead of the retainer — including as its own cold offer: "Not asking for a retainer. One week, one workflow, $650, you keep it either way." End each sprint with a before/after Loom and a one-page ROI sheet, then propose the retainer as "sprints, continuously."

**Time:** 2–3 hrs/week for ~2 weeks to build, then it's just delivery.

**Timeline:** Shortens every other channel's sales cycle by 2–4 weeks.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** A $3–4k/month retainer is an impossible first yes for a service the buyer can't picture and isn't sure works *for them*. A cheap, bounded, keep-the-result sprint converts "I don't get it" into "fine, show me" — and the sprint's before/after numbers become your retainer proposal. Honest tradeoff: lower margin, and some buyers are DIY-ers who never convert. Expect 40–60% sprint-to-retainer; price the sprint assuming some won't, and only target businesses big enough to need ongoing work.

---

## 8. Niche industry newsletter sponsorships (the one cheap paid play)
*$150–600 per send · Near-zero ongoing time*

**What to do:** Find the newsletters owners in your vertical actually read — trade association newsletters, independent industry Substacks/beehiiv publications. Buy 2–3 small sends across 2 newsletters promoting ONE thing: the workshop (#4) or the sprint (#7), with an angle like "The 6 hours your office manager loses every Friday." Track with a dedicated booking link.

**Time:** 1–2 hrs/week for two weeks, then almost nothing.

**Timeline:** 3–6 weeks.

**Why it works for AI specifically:** This is not Google Ads, which is priced for venture-backed SaaS bidding on "AI consulting." Nobody is selling AI implementation in a newsletter for roofers, so you're the only signal in the channel. The math: a $400 send reaching 3,000 owners only needs to produce one client per ~1,500 sends to beat your margins. Never buy annual packages — test single sends, because list quality varies wildly.

---

## How I'd sequence the 6 months

- **Weeks 1–2:** Define the sprint (#7), launch #1 and #2. ~9 hrs/week.
- **Weeks 3–6:** Add #3 and #4 as #1's list runs dry.
- **Ongoing:** Layer #5, #6, #8 as bandwidth allows — these are your months-3-through-6 pipeline.

You need 5 closes, which realistically means 15–25 qualified conversations across all channels. This plan generates that volume, but don't run all eight at once — you'll do everything at 40% quality.

One flag you didn't ask about: 8 clients at your current delivery model is roughly 2.7x your current load with one contractor. The sprint model conveniently stress-tests your delivery capacity *before* prospects become retainers — but it's worth pressure-testing now whether the constraint at month 5 is leads or hours.
